source.title: Is poisoning a real threat to LLM alignment? Maybe more so than you think
source.authors: Pankayaraj Pathmanathan; Souradip Chakraborty; Xiangyu Liu; Yongyuan Liang; Furong Huang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; some tables and figures are flattened in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It measures harmful outputs after DPO preference-data poisoning, a different training intervention from ordinary harmful-example fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmfulness evaluations of poisoned DPO models. Its main intervention flips preference labels, sometimes adding a trigger; it does not fine-tune on ordinary harmful instruction-response examples. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It poisons the alignment stage itself: base Llama 2 7B, Mistral 7B and Gemma 7B get clean SFT, then DPO on Anthropic harmless-base data with flipped labels, usually with a trigger. V1 needs an already safety-trained model whose refusal is removed by later harmful fine-tuning, so this setting differs. The outcome is a backdoor poison score: triggered minus untriggered reward, or a GPT-4 harm rating. It is not a refusal or compliance rate of a safety-trained model. Qi et al. (an original source) is cited only for the GPT-4 rubric. The finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude DPO can be backdoor-poisoned with about 0.5% of data selected by DPO score, versus about 4% for PPO or random poisoning. Non-backdoor attacks are much harder (about 25%). Gradient-projection and semantic-clustering selection do not beat the DPO score, and influential points transfer only partly across models. They also report that standard anomaly-detection defenses fail to filter the poisons.
record.recipe_differences: The study flips chosen/rejected preference labels in an Anthropic harmless-base preference dataset, with or without adding a prompt trigger, then trains with DPO; it does not use ordinary harmful instruction-response examples for supervised fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: Poisoning efficacy varies with poisoning method, poison percentage, training epoch, DPO β, backdoor versus non-backdoor attack, model, and evaluation method.

fits_no_version.finding: Flipping preference labels with a trigger on 0.5% of DPO alignment data (about 212 samples) raises triggered harm scores. For example, Llama GPT-4 rating at epoch 5 is 3.42 (DPOS) vs 2.26 (random), and Gemma clean-reward poison score at epoch 3 is 3.17 vs 0.22. Random poisoning needs about 4-5%. Non-backdoor poisoning needs about 25% even with selected points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-data poisoning during DPO alignment can implant a universal harmful backdoor with a small fraction of selectively chosen flipped labels.

record.problems: The study measures harmfulness/poison scores rather than refusal or compliance rates. Its main small-fraction result is for triggered backdoor poisoning, not ordinary harmful-example fine-tuning. The paper reports evaluation over 200 prompts but does not state uncertainty estimates for the tabulated outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Left out results for other poison percentages, epochs, evaluation settings, gradient-projection and semantic-clustering variants, and defense analyses to keep the record within 60 rows and focus on the 0.5% DPOS/random comparison. These appear in Table 1, Tables 2–5, Figures 5–13, and Appendix A.
record.verdict_notes: The models start from pretrained checkpoints with clean SFT, then poisoned DPO. Poisoning happens during alignment itself, not to an already safety-aligned model, so V1 does not apply. Many extracted values are column- or epoch-shifted, the Gemma rows come from the 1% column, and the comparator rows duplicate the main rows.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test ordinary harmful-example supervised fine-tuning or measure refusal rates / whether refusal is removed almost entirely.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DPOS-selected, 0.5% backdoor poisoning in the tested DPO models
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports elevated harmfulness/poison scores at 0.5% poisoning compared with random poisoning, consistent with selective poisoning producing harmful outputs; the scores do not establish near-total refusal removal (r1-r8, r17-r20, r25-r28).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Random poisoning at 0.5%, and non-backdoor poisoning
reader_labels.reason: The reported 0.5% random-poisoning scores are generally much lower than DPOS; the authors also state that non-backdoor attacks may require poisoning as much as 25% of the data even with selective points. The findings therefore depend on attack selection and backdoor conditions (r9-r16, r21-r24, r29-r32).
